title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 822–824 (Night 178, continuing nights-177), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 178 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The ifrit Dahnash, having accepted the jinniya Maymūna's condition, tells her what he saw that night in the islands of the land of China, the realm of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands, the seas and the seven palaces: a daughter more beautiful than any God created in her time. Saying that his tongue cannot do her justice, he gives a description by approximation, head to foot, in rhymed prose broken by three short pieces of verse: hair like the nights of separation and a face like the days of union, a nose like a polished sword-edge, cheeks of wine-red, lips of coral and carnelian, a tongue moved by ample wit and a ready answer, a bosom that tempts whoever sees it, braceleted arms, breasts like two ivory caskets, a belly folded like figured Coptic linen, a waist slender as a fancy, hips so heavy they keep her seated when she would rise and wake her when she would sleep, and small feet that make him wonder how they bear what is above them. He cuts the description short for fear of going on too long — and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-eighth night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-thāmina, “the eighth”, feminine to agree with layla. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ دَهْنَشًا قَالَ لِمَيْمُونَةَ رَضِيتُ يَا سَيِّدَتِى بِهٰذَا الشَّرْطِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Dahnashan qāla li-Maymūnata raḍītu yā sayyidatī bi-hādhā al-sharṭi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Dahnash said to-Maymūna: I-have-accepted, O my-lady, this the-condition.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Dahnash said to Maymūna, “I accept this condition, my lady.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks up the last words of the previous night. After anna the name is accusative, and the print spells it دهنشا, with the alif of the indefinite accusative, Dahnashan, treating the name as fully declinable. Maymūna, a feminine name, is diptote, so after li-, “to”, it takes -a: li-Maymūnata. raḍiya bi-, “to accept, be content with”: bi- marks what is accepted. The print writes سيدتي as سيدتى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ اعْلَمِي يَا سَيِّدَتِي أَنِّي قَدْ خَرَجْتُ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ مِنَ الْجَزَائِرِ الدَّاخِلَةِ فِي بِلَادِ الصِّينِ وَهِيَ بِلَادُ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ صَاحِبِ الْجَزَائِرِ وَالْبُحُورِ وَالسَّبْعَةِ قُصُورٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla iʿlamī yā sayyidatī annī qad kharajtu fī hādhihi al-laylati mina al-jazāʾiri al-dākhilati fī bilādi al-Ṣīni wa-hiya bilādu al-maliki al-Ghayūri ṣāḥibi al-jazāʾiri wa-al-buḥūri wa-al-sabʿati quṣūrin
sentences.l: Then he-said: Know, O my-lady, that-I have gone-out in this the-night from the-islands, the-lying-within (the) lands (of) China, and-they (are the) lands (of) the-king al-Ghayūr, lord (of) the-islands and-the-seas and-the-seven palaces.
sentences.i: Then he said, “Know, my lady, that tonight I came out of the islands that lie within the lands of China, the lands of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands and the seas and the seven palaces.
sentences.n: kharajtu … mina al-jazāʾiri, “I came out from the islands”: Dahnash is reporting where he has just flown from. al-dākhila fī, “entering into, lying within”, active participle of dakhala. al-Ghayūr, “the Jealous”, an intensive form from ghayra, “jealousy”, is the king's name or epithet. The rhyme runs al-Ghayūri / al-buḥūri / quṣūrin; buḥūr, a less common plural of baḥr, “sea”, beside biḥār, serves the rhyme. al-sabʿati quṣūrin, “the seven palaces”, puts the article on the numeral and leaves the counted noun indefinite, a Middle Arabic habit; Classical would say al-quṣūri al-sabʿati or sabʿati al-quṣūri. Here the print writes سيدتي with its dots, where the line before had سيدتى. The ئ of الجزائر is printed both times.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ لِذٰلِكَ الْمَلِكِ بِنْتًا لَمْ يَخْلُقِ اللّٰهُ فِي زَمَانِهَا أَحْسَنَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu li-dhālika al-maliki bintan lam yakhluqi Allāhu fī zamānihā aḥsana minhā
sentences.l: And-I-saw to-that the-king a-daughter; not created God in her-time (one) more-beautiful than-her.
sentences.i: And I saw that this king had a daughter; in her time God has created none more beautiful than she.
sentences.n: li-dhālika al-maliki, “belonging to that king”: li- of possession, so “I saw that the king had a daughter”. lam yakhluqi Allāhu … aḥsana minhā, “God did not create … one more beautiful than her”: the elative aḥsan is the object, and min after it means “than”; the -i of yakhluqi is a helping vowel before the article. The أ of فرأيت is printed.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي لَمْ أَقْدِرْ أَصِفُهَا لَكَ فَإِنَّ لِسَانِي يَعْجِزُ عَنْ وَصْفِهَا كَمَايَنْبَغِي وَلٰكِنْ أَذْكُرُلَكَ شَيْأً مِنْ صِفَاتِهَا عَلَى سَبِيلِ التَّقْرِيبِ
sentences.tr: wa-innī lam aqdir aṣifuhā laka fa-inna lisānī yaʿjizu ʿan waṣfihā kamā yanbaghī wa-lākin adhkuru laka shayʾan min ṣifātihā ʿalā sabīli al-taqrībi
sentences.l: And-indeed-I, not I-was-able I-describe-her to-you, for indeed my-tongue falls-short of describing-her as-is-fitting; but I-tell-you something of her-qualities by (the) way (of) the-bringing-near.
sentences.i: I cannot describe her to you, for my tongue falls short of describing her as she deserves; but I will tell you something of her charms, by way of approximation.
sentences.n: lam aqdir aṣifuhā, “I was not able, I describe her”: the second verb follows the first directly, in the indicative, with no an, “to”, between them; Classical would say lam aqdir an aṣifahā. This loose chaining of verbs is common in the later language. ʿajaza ʿan, “to fall short of, be unable for”. The print runs كما ينبغي together as كماينبغي and اذكر لك as اذكرلك, and the spacing is kept: read kamā yanbaghī, “as is fitting”, and adhkuru laka, “I tell you”. ʿalā sabīli al-taqrībi, “by way of bringing (it) near”, that is, roughly, as an approximation. شيأ, with the hamza on the alif, is the print's spelling of shayʾan; the أ is printed.

sentences.t: أَمَّا شَعْرُهَا فَكَلَيَالِي الْهَجْرِ وَالِانْفِصَالِ وَأَمَّا وَجْهُهَا فَكَأَيَّامِ الْوِصَالِ وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ فِي وَصْفِهَا مَنْ قَالَ
sentences.tr: ammā shaʿruhā fa-ka-layālī al-hajri wa-al-infiṣāli wa-ammā wajhuhā fa-ka-ayyāmi al-wiṣāli wa-qad aḥsana fī waṣfihā man qāla
sentences.l: As-for her-hair, (it is) like-(the)-nights (of) the-forsaking and-the-parting; and-as-for her-face, (it is) like-(the)-days (of) the-union. And-indeed did-well in describing-her (he) who said:
sentences.i: As for her hair, it is like the nights of estrangement and parting; as for her face, it is like the days when lovers are united. And well did he describe her who said:
sentences.n: The set-piece begins, in rhymed prose: al-infiṣāli / al-wiṣāli. ammā … fa-, “as for … then”: fa- opens the answer, and ka-, “like”, is the kāf of comparison, here and all through the description. The nights of separation are long and black, like her hair; the days of union are bright, like her face. hajr, “forsaking, estrangement”, and wiṣāl, “union”, are the two poles of Arabic love poetry. aḥsana fī waṣfihā, “did well in describing her”, has its subject, man qāla, “he who said”, put last to lead into the verse. The fatḥa of مَن is printed.

sentences.t:
نَشَرَتْ ثَلْثُ ذَوائِبِ مِنْ شَعْرِهَا * فِيْ لَيْلَةٍ فَاَرَتْ لَيَالِيَ اَرْبَعًا
وَاسْتَقْبَلَتْ قَمَرَ السَّمَاءِ بِوَجْهِهَا * فَاَرَتْنِيَ الْقَمَرَيْنِ فِي وَقْتٍ مَعًا
sentences.tr:
nasharat thalthu dhawāʾibi min shaʿrihā * fī laylatin fa-arat layāliya arbaʿan
wa-istaqbalat qamara al-samāʾi bi-wajhihā * fa-aratniya al-qamarayni fī waqtin maʿan
sentences.l:
She-spread-out three locks of her-hair * in a-night, and-showed nights four;
and-she-faced (the) moon (of) the-sky with-her-face * and-showed-me the-two-moons at one-time together.
sentences.i:
She let down three tresses of her hair one night, and showed four nights;
she turned her face to the moon in the sky, and showed me two moons at once.
sentences.n: Two lines in the kāmil metre, rhyming in -ʿā. The conceit is arithmetic: three black tresses and the night itself make four nights; her face and the moon make two moons. al-qamarān, “the two moons”, usually means the sun and the moon; here it is the moon and her face. arat, “she showed”, is the perfect of arā, Form IV of raʾā, “to see”; in fa-aratniya the object pronoun -nī, “me”, takes its older form -niya, with a fatḥa, for the metre. The marks are the print's, copied as they stand. ثَلْثُ is the edition's short spelling of thalāth, “three” (as it writes ثلثة), but its pointing, with a sukūn and a nominative ending, does not scan: the metre wants thalātha dhawāʾibin, object of nasharat, with the counted noun given tanwīn by poetic licence. The print has ذَوائِبِ, with a printed ئ and no tanwīn. Also the print's: the sukūn on the long vowel of فِيْ, and the vowel on a bare alif with no hamza sign in فَاَرَتْ, اَرْبَعًا and فَاَرَتْنِيَ.

sentences.t: وَلَهَا أَنْفٌ كَحَدِّ السَّيْفِ الْمَصْقُولِ وَلَهَا وَجْنَتَانِ كَرَحِيقِ الْأُرْجُوَانِ وَلَهَا خَدٌّ كَشَقَائِقِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lahā anfun ka-ḥaddi al-sayfi al-maṣqūli wa-lahā wajnatāni ka-raḥīqi al-urjuwāni wa-lahā khaddun ka-shaqāʾiqi al-nuʿmāni
sentences.l: And-to-her (is) a-nose like-(the)-edge (of) the-sword the-polished; and-to-her (are) two-cheeks like-(the)-wine (of) the-purple; and-to-her (is) a-cheek like-(the)-anemones (of) the-Nuʿmān.
sentences.i: She has a nose like the edge of a polished sword, cheeks like purple wine, and a cheek like the red anemone.
sentences.n: Each feature is set out with wa-lahā, “and to her (is)”, the li- of possession: “she has”. ka- is the kāf of comparison each time. The rhyme falls on al-urjuwāni / al-nuʿmāni; al-maṣqūli stands outside it. wajna and khadd both mean “cheek”: wajna is properly the rounded upper cheek, khadd the cheek as a whole, so the text can give her both. urjuwān, “purple, red-purple”, is a loanword from Persian; raḥīq al-urjuwān is perhaps “purple wine”, the colour of the flush. shaqāʾiq al-nuʿmān, literally “the shaqāʾiq of al-Nuʿmān”, is the red wild anemone, a stock image for cheeks. The shadda of خدّ and the ئ of كشقائق are printed.

sentences.t: وَشَفَتَاهَا كَالْمَرْجَانِ وَالْعَقِيقِ وَرِيقُهَا أَشْهَى مِنَ الرَّحِيقِ يُطْفِئُ مَذَاقُهُ عَذَابَ الْحَرِيقِ
sentences.tr: wa-shafatāhā ka-al-marjāni wa-al-ʿaqīqi wa-rīquhā ashhā mina al-raḥīqi yuṭfiʾu madhāquhu ʿadhāba al-ḥarīqi
sentences.l: And-her-two-lips (are) like-the-coral and-the-carnelian, and-her-saliva (is) more-delicious than the-choice-wine; quenches its-taste (the) torment (of) the-burning.
sentences.i: Her lips are like coral and carnelian, and the taste of her mouth is sweeter than choice wine: it puts out the torment of the fire.
sentences.n: Three rhymes in -īq: al-ʿaqīqi / al-raḥīqi / al-ḥarīqi. shafatāhā, “her two lips”, is the dual with its -n dropped before the suffix. ʿaqīq is carnelian, the red stone. rīq, “saliva”, the lover's drink in Arabic poetry, is frankly the taste of her mouth in kissing; raḥīq is pure, choice wine. ashhā min, “more desirable than”, is the elative of shahiya, “to desire”. yuṭfiʾu, “quenches, puts out”, is Form IV of ṭafiʾa; ʿadhāb al-ḥarīq, “the torment of burning”, is the fire of love, and the phrase is also the Qurʾān's for the punishment of hellfire. The ئ of يطفئ is printed.

sentences.t: وَلِسَانُهَا يُحَرِّكُهُ عَقْلٌ وَافِرٌ وَجَوَابٌ حَاضِرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lisānuhā yuḥarrikuhu ʿaqlun wāfirun wa-jawābun ḥāḍirun
sentences.l: And-her-tongue, moves-it an-intelligence abundant and-an-answer ready.
sentences.i: Her tongue is set moving by ample wit and a ready answer.
sentences.n: The print has وجراب, “and a bag”, a misprint for وجواب, “and an answer”, corrected here: jawābun ḥāḍirun, “a ready answer”, pairs with ʿaqlun wāfirun, “abundant intelligence”, and rhymes with it, wāfirun / ḥāḍirun. The topic lisānuhā, “her tongue”, comes first and is picked up by the pronoun -hu of yuḥarrikuhu, “moves it”. The shadda of يحرّكه is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَهَا صَدْرٌ فِتْنَةٌ لِمَنْ يَرَاهُ فَسُبْحَانَ مَنْ خَلَقَهُ وَسَوَّاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lahā ṣadrun fitnatun li-man yarāhu fa-subḥāna man khalaqahu wa-sawwāhu
sentences.l: And-to-her (is) a-breast, a-temptation for-whoever sees-it; so-glory (to the One) who created-it and-fashioned-it.
sentences.i: She has a bosom that tempts whoever looks on it: glory to Him who made it and shaped it!
sentences.n: ṣadrun fitnatun, “a breast, a temptation”: the second noun describes the first, as if it were an adjective. li-man yarāhu, “for whoever sees it”: li- marks the one tempted. subḥāna man, “glory to (Him) who”, is the exclamation of wonder at God's handiwork; khalaqa … wa-sawwā, “created … and fashioned (in due proportion)”, echoes the Qurʾān (87:2, 82:7). Rhyme: yarāhu / sawwāhu. The shadda of وسوّاه is printed.

sentences.t: وَ مُتَّصِلٌ بِهِ عَضُدَانِ مُدَمْلَجَانِ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِمَا الشَّاعِرُ الْوَلْهَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-muttaṣilun bihi ʿaḍudāni mudamlajāni kamā qāla fīhimā al-shāʿiru al-walhānu
sentences.l: And joined to-it (are) two-upper-arms, rounded, as said about-them-two the-poet, the-love-crazed:
sentences.i: Joined to it are two smooth, rounded upper arms, as the love-crazed poet said of them:
sentences.n: The print ends its line with a lone و and begins the next with متصل; the spacing is kept, and the two read together as wa-muttaṣilun, “and joined”. The participle muttaṣil, from ittaṣala bi-, “to be joined to” (bi- marks what a thing is joined to; here the bosom), comes first, in the singular, as a fronted predicate may before its dual subject ʿaḍudāni, “two upper arms”. mudamlaj, related to dumluj, “armlet”, is “rounded and smooth”, as though turned for an armlet. Rhyme: mudamlajāni / al-walhānu; walhān, “distraught with love”.

sentences.t: وَزَنْدَانِ لَوْ لَا اُمْسِكَ بِاَسَاوِرٍ * لَسَالَ مِنَ الْاَكْمَامِ سَيْلَ الْجَدَاوِلِ
sentences.tr: wa-zandāni law lā umsika bi-asāwirin * la-sāla mina al-akmāmi sayla al-jadāwili
sentences.l: And-two-forearms, if not (it) was-held with-bracelets, * surely-would-have-flowed from the-sleeves (the) flowing (of) the-streams.
sentences.i: And forearms which, had the bracelets not held them in, would have run out of her sleeves as brooks run.
sentences.n: One line in the ṭawīl metre. zand is the forearm, strictly the bone where the bracelet sits; the dual zandāni opens the line without a verb, “(and she has) two forearms”. They are so soft and smooth that they would pour out of her sleeves like water if the bracelets did not hold them. The print splits لولا as لَوْ لَا, so it reads as law with the negative lā, “if … not”, before a past verb, “had (they) not been held”; Classical lawlā takes a noun, “were it not for”, and law lam a verb, and the line mixes the two. umsika is a singular passive with a dual subject, and the metre falters at that word: the dual umsikā would scan, but the print has اُمْسِكَ, and it is kept. la- in la-sāla introduces the answer of law, “(then) it would have flowed”. sayla al-jadāwili, “the flowing of the streams”, is a cognate accusative: it would flow as streams flow. bi- marks what holds them, “by bracelets”; asāwir, plural of siwār, “bracelet”, is diptote in prose, and the tanwīn of بِاَسَاوِرٍ is poetic licence, which the metre needs. The marks are the print's, including the vowel on a bare alif in اُمْسِكَ, بِاَسَاوِرٍ and الْاَكْمَامِ.

sentences.t: وَلَهَا نَهْدَانِ كَأَنَّهُمَا مِنَ الْعَاجِ حُقَّانِ يَسْتَمِدُّ مِنْ إِشْرَاقِهِمَا الْقَمَرَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lahā nahdāni ka-annahumā mina al-ʿāji ḥuqqāni yastamiddu min ishrāqihimā al-qamarāni
sentences.l: And-to-her (are) two-breasts, as-if-they-two (were), of the-ivory, two-caskets; draw-supply from their-shining the-two-moons.
sentences.i: She has two breasts like two little caskets of ivory, from whose radiance the sun and the moon draw their light.
sentences.n: ka-annahumā … ḥuqqāni, “as though they were two caskets”: ka-anna, “as though”, puts the pronoun -humā in the accusative, and the predicate ḥuqqāni follows, with mina al-ʿāji, “of ivory”, the material, set before it. ḥuqq (also ḥuqqa) is a small round lidded box, of the kind turned in ivory for perfume or jewels; the comparison of breasts with ivory caskets is an old one in Arabic poetry. yastamiddu min, “to draw supply from”, is Form X of madda; al-qamarān, “the two moons”, are the sun and the moon, which take their light from her. The singular verb before a dual subject is Classical. Rhyme: ḥuqqāni / al-qamarāni. The shaddas of حقّان and يستمدّ are printed.

sentences.t: وَلَهَا بَطْنٌ بِأَعْكَانٍ مَطْوِيَّةٍ كَطَيِّ الْقَبَاطِى الْمِصْرِيَّةِ الْمُدَبَّجَةِ بِطَيَّاتٍ كَالْقَرَاطِيسِ الْمُدْرَجَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-lahā baṭnun bi-aʿkānin maṭwiyyatin ka-ṭayyi al-qabāṭī al-miṣriyyati al-mudabbajati bi-ṭayyātin ka-al-qarāṭīsi al-mudrajati
sentences.l: And-to-her (is) a-belly with-folds, folded like-(the)-folding (of) the-Coptic-linens the-Egyptian, the-figured, with-pleats like-the-papers the-rolled-up.
sentences.i: She has a belly with soft folds, folded like fine Egyptian linen, figured with pleats like rolled sheets of paper.
sentences.n: باعكان is bi-aʿkānin, “with folds”, bi- of accompaniment. aʿkān is the plural of ʿukna, a fold of flesh on the belly, a mark of beauty in a well-fed woman; the folds are maṭwiyya, “folded”, feminine singular to agree with a plural of things. ka-ṭayyi, “like the folding of”, is the kāf of comparison with the verbal noun of ṭawā, “to fold”. al-qabāṭī, plural of qubṭiyya, are the fine white linen cloths of Egypt, named after the Copts; the print writes the final ي as ى. al-mudabbaja, “figured, ornamented”, from dībāj, “brocade”, agrees with al-qabāṭī; whether bi-ṭayyātin, “with pleats”, goes with mudabbaja, “figured with pleats”, or with the belly itself is not clear. qarāṭīs, plural of qirṭās, are sheets of paper or papyrus, and mudraja, “rolled, folded up”. Rhyme: maṭwiyyatin / al-miṣriyyati, then al-mudabbajati / al-mudrajati. The shaddas of مطويّة, كطيّ and طيّات are printed.

sentences.t: وَيَنْتَهِي ذٰلِكَ إِلَى خَصْرٍ مُخْتَصَرٍ مِنْ وَهْمِ الْخَيَّالِ فَوْقَ رِدْفٍ كَكَثِيبٍ مِنْ رِمَالٍ يُقْعِدُهَا إِذَا أَرَادَتِ الْقِيَامَ وَيُوقِظُهَا إِذَا أَرَادَتِ الْمَنَامَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهَا الشَّاعِرُ وَأَجَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-yantahī dhālika ilā khaṣrin mukhtaṣarin min wahmi al-khayyāli fawqa ridfin ka-kathībin min rimālin yuqʿiduhā idhā arādati al-qiyāma wa-yūqiẓuhā idhā arādati al-manāma kamā qāla fīhā al-shāʿiru wa-ajāda
sentences.l: And-ends that at a-waist abridged, out-of (the) fancy (of) the-imaginer, above a-rump like-a-dune of sands; it-seats-her when she-wants the-rising, and-wakes-her when she-wants the-sleeping; as said about-her the-poet, and-did-excellently:
sentences.i: That runs down to a waist so slight it seems a thing of fancy, above haunches like a hill of sand, which pull her down when she would rise and keep her awake when she would sleep; as the poet said of her, and said it well:
sentences.n: khaṣrun mukhtaṣarun, “a waist abridged”, plays on two words from the same root, kh-ṣ-r: the waist is so slender it is a shortened thing. min wahmi al-khayyāli is not certain: wahm is “fancy, imagining”, and the phrase most likely says that the waist is made of fancy, or is slimmer than fancy itself. The print sets a shadda on الخيّال, which makes khayyāl, “horseman”, or an intensive “one given to imagining”; one expects khayāl, “phantom, figment”, and the shadda may be the compositor's, but it is printed and kept. ridf, “rump, haunches”; kathīb, “a heap or dune of sand”, is the standard image for heavy hips. Their weight keeps her sitting when she wants to stand and, it seems, gives her no rest when she wants to sleep. Rhymes: al-khayyāli / rimālin, al-qiyāma / al-manāma. ajāda, “he did it excellently”, is Form IV of jāda.

sentences.t:
لَهَا كَفَلٌ تَعَلَّقَ فِيْ ضَعِيْفِ * وَذَاكَ الرِّدْفُ لِيْ وَلَهَا ظَلُوْمُ
فَيُوْقِفُنِيْ اِذَا فَكَّرْتُ فِيْهِ * وَيُقْعِدُهَا اِذَا هَمَّتْ تَقُوْمُ
sentences.tr:
lahā kafalun taʿallaqa fī ḍaʿīfi * wa-dhāka al-ridfu lī wa-lahā ẓalūmu
fa-yūqifunī idhā fakkartu fīhi * wa-yuqʿiduhā idhā hammat taqūmu
sentences.l:
To-her (is) a-buttock (that) hung on a-frail-(one), * and-that the-rump, to-me and-to-her (is) a-wrongdoer;
for-it-makes-me-stand when I-think about-it, * and-makes-her-sit when she-is-minded she-rises.
sentences.i:
She has buttocks hung upon something frail, and those haunches wrong us both, me and her:
when I think of them they make me stand, and when she would rise they sit her down.
sentences.n: Two lines in the wāfir metre, rhyming in -ūmu. kafal and ridf both mean “buttocks, haunches”. taʿallaqa fī ḍaʿīfi, “it hung on a weak (thing)”: the weak thing is the waist. Classical would have taʿallaqa bi- or min, and an indefinite ḍaʿīfin with tanwīn; the print points ḍaʿīfi with a bare kasra, and that is kept. ẓalūm, “very unjust”, is an intensive form that serves for both genders; lī wa-lahā, “to me and to her”: li- marks the one wronged. The second line turns on the double sense of yūqifunī, “it makes me stand”: he starts up at the thought, and, plainly, it gives him an erection; meanwhile the same weight sits her down. idhā hammat taqūmu, “when she is minded, she rises”: Classical says hammat an taqūma, “she was about to rise”, or hammat bi-al-qiyāmi; here the verb follows bare, in the indicative, held by the rhyme. The marks are the print's, including the sukūn on long vowels (فِيْ, ضَعِيْفِ, لِيْ, ظَلُوْمُ, فَيُوْقِفُنِيْ, فِيْهِ, تَقُوْمُ) and the kasra on a bare alif in اِذَا.

sentences.t: وَيَحْمِلُ ذٰلِكَ الْكَفَلَ فَخِذَانِ مُدَمْلَجَانِ وَسَاقَانِ كَأَنَّهُمَا مِنَ الدُّرِّ عَمُودَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-yaḥmilu dhālika al-kafala fakhidhāni mudamlajāni wa-sāqāni ka-annahumā mina al-durri ʿamūdāni
sentences.l: And-carry that the-buttock two-thighs, rounded, and-two-shanks, as-if-they-two (were), of the-pearl, two-columns.
sentences.i: That buttock is borne up by two smooth, rounded thighs, and by two legs like columns of pearl.
sentences.n: The object, dhālika al-kafala, “that buttock”, comes before the subject, fakhidhāni, “two thighs”, and the verb is singular before the dual subject, as Classical allows. mudamlaj, as of the arms above, “rounded, well-turned”. sāq, “shank, lower leg”. ka-annahumā mina al-durri ʿamūdāni, “as though they were two columns of pearl”, is built like the ivory caskets of the breasts. Rhyme: mudamlajāni / ʿamūdāni. The shadda of الدرّ is printed.

sentences.t: وَيَحْمِلُ ذٰلِكَ كُلَّهُ قَدَمَانِ لَطِيفَانِ مُحَدَّدَانِ مِثْلَ حَدِّ السِّنَانِ صَنْعَةُ الْمُهَيْمِنِ الدَّيَّانِ
sentences.tr: wa-yaḥmilu dhālika kullahu qadamāni laṭīfāni muḥaddadāni mithla ḥaddi al-sināni ṣanʿatu al-muhaymini al-dayyāni
sentences.l: And-carry that all-of-it two-feet, dainty, tapered like (the) edge (of) the-spearhead, (the) work (of) the-Watcher-over-all, the-Requiter.
sentences.i: And all of this is carried on two dainty feet, tapering like the point of a spear, the handiwork of the All-Watching, the Judge.
sentences.n: qadam, “foot”, is usually feminine, but its adjectives here are masculine, laṭīfāni, muḥaddadāni; Classical would say laṭīfatāni. muḥaddad, “sharpened, made pointed”, is Form II from ḥadd, “edge”, which follows: mithla ḥaddi al-sināni, “like the edge of the spearhead”, that is, small and narrow. ṣanʿatu, “the handiwork of”, is read as a nominative standing on its own, “(they are) the work of”; it could also be taken as an accusative of praise. al-Muhaymin, “the Guardian, the One who watches over all”, and al-Dayyān, “the Requiter, the Judge”, are both names of God. Rhymes: laṭīfāni / muḥaddadāni / al-sināni / al-dayyāni. The shaddas of محدّدان, حدّ and الديّان are printed.

sentences.t: فَعَجِبْتُ لِصِغَرِهِمَا كَيْفَ يَحْمِلَانِ مَا فَوْقَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿajibtu li-ṣigharihimā kayfa yaḥmilāni mā fawqahumā
sentences.l: And-I-marvelled at-their-two-smallness, how they-two-carry what (is) above-them-two.
sentences.i: I marvelled that feet so small could carry all that was above them.
sentences.n: ʿajiba li-, “to wonder at”: li- marks what causes the wonder, here ṣigar, “smallness”. The dual pronoun -humā and the dual verb yaḥmilāni, “they two carry”, refer back to the feet.

sentences.t: وَقَدِ اخْتَصَرْتُ فِي وَصْفِهَا خَوْفَ الْإِطَالَةِ فَتَرَكْتُهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qadi ikhtaṣartu fī waṣfihā khawfa al-iṭālati fa-taraktuhu
sentences.l: And-indeed I-have-abridged in describing-her (for) fear (of) the-lengthening, so-I-left-it.
sentences.i: I have cut short my description of her for fear of going on too long, and so I leave it there.”
sentences.n: khawfa al-iṭālati, “for fear of going on at length”: khawf is an accusative of reason. ikhtaṣara, “to abridge, be brief”, is Form VIII of the root of khaṣr, “waist”, and mukhtaṣar just above. fa-taraktuhu, “and so I left it”, is read as Dahnash's own words, the -hu, “it”, being the description, waṣf, which is masculine; the word is a little abrupt, and might be read otherwise, but nothing else before it fits the masculine pronoun as well. qadi takes a helping -i before the joining alif.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula. Shahrazāda is the object, put before the subject al-ṣabāḥu, and the rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
